title: Espresso Martini Hangover: Why It Hits Harder and What Helps
excerpt: Why espresso martini hangovers feel so rough: hidden alcohol per glass, caffeine that masks drunkenness, wrecked sleep, and what actually helps before and after.
metaDescription: Why espresso martini hangovers hit hard: about 1.4 drinks per glass, caffeine that masks how drunk you are, and broken sleep. How to prevent and recover.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** an espresso martini hangover usually isn't caused by anything magical in the coffee. It comes from the same thing every hangover comes from, which is alcohol, plus three things this particular drink adds on top. Each cocktail carries more alcohol than people assume (roughly one and a half standard drinks). The caffeine makes you feel more awake than you really are, which makes it easy to order a third and fourth. And the late-night caffeine cuts into your sleep, so you wake up tired, foggy, and sometimes jittery on top of the usual headache and nausea. The sugar plays a smaller role than its reputation suggests.

**The quick rules:** Count each espresso martini as about one and a half drinks, not one. Don't use the caffeine as a reason to keep going, because it doesn't make you less drunk. Stop ordering them a few hours before you plan to sleep. Alternate with water, eat a real meal, and if you wake up with a headache, have a normal cup of coffee rather than skipping it, since caffeine withdrawal can make a hangover headache worse.

> **When to see a doctor.** A rough morning after a few cocktails is normal and passes on its own. Get medical help **right away** (call 911 in the US) if someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting repeatedly, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has pale, bluish, or cold skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and the caffeine in an espresso martini does not protect against it. Also see a doctor if you have chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle within an hour or two of resting, fainting, or vomiting blood. If you have a heart rhythm condition, high blood pressure, anxiety disorder, or take stimulant medication, ask your doctor whether caffeine-and-alcohol drinks are a good idea for you.

## What's Actually in an Espresso Martini

The drink was created in London in the 1980s by bartender Dick Bradsell, and the modern version is pretty consistent from bar to bar. A typical recipe looks like this:

| Ingredient | Typical amount | What it contributes |
|---|---|---|
| Vodka | 45 to 60 ml (1.5 to 2 oz) | Most of the alcohol |
| Coffee liqueur (Kahlúa or similar) | 20 to 30 ml (about 1 oz) | More alcohol, lots of sugar, a little caffeine |
| Fresh espresso | One shot, about 30 ml | Most of the caffeine |
| Sugar syrup | 0 to 15 ml | Extra sugar, depending on the bar |

Shaken hard with ice, that's the whole drink. It tastes like dessert and goes down fast, which is exactly the problem.

### How much alcohol is that?

A US standard drink contains about 14 grams of pure alcohol, which is what you get in a 12-ounce beer at 5%, a 5-ounce glass of wine, or a 1.5-ounce shot of 40% spirits.

A classic espresso martini with 50 ml of vodka at 40% and 25 ml of coffee liqueur at about 20% works out to roughly 19 to 20 grams of alcohol. That's about **1.4 standard drinks** in a glass that looks small and tastes sweet. A generous pour, a stronger liqueur, or a double-sized "house special" can push it closer to two.

So three espresso martinis is not three drinks. It's closer to four or five. Most people don't count it that way, and that gap between what you think you drank and what you actually drank explains a lot of bad mornings.

### How much caffeine is that?

One shot of espresso usually contains somewhere around 60 to 75 mg of caffeine, depending on the beans and how it's pulled. Coffee liqueur adds a small extra amount. So one espresso martini is roughly similar to a small cup of coffee. Two or three of them in an evening adds up to about what many people drink in a full morning, except you're taking it at 10 or 11 at night.

## Why Espresso Martini Hangovers Feel So Bad

There's no single cause. It's several smaller ones stacking up.

### 1. The caffeine hides how drunk you are

This is the most important point, and it's the one most people get backwards. Caffeine does not speed up how fast your liver clears alcohol, and it doesn't lower your blood alcohol level. What it does is make you *feel* more alert. Alcohol makes you sleepy, and sleepiness is one of the body's natural signals that it's time to stop. Caffeine blunts that signal.

The CDC describes this directly in its guidance on mixing alcohol and caffeine: caffeine can mask alcohol's depressant effects, so people feel less drunk than they are and may drink more than they otherwise would. Lab research on alcohol mixed with energy drinks, including work by Cecile Marczinski and Mark Fillmore at the University of Kentucky, found that adding caffeine made people *rate* themselves as less impaired while their actual reaction times and motor control were still impaired by the alcohol. Researchers sometimes call this being "wide awake drunk."

Most of that research was done with energy drinks rather than espresso, so the exact numbers don't carry over. But the basic pharmacology is the same caffeine. The practical result is simple: the person who would have gone home after two vodka sodas stays out for four espresso martinis, and the hangover reflects four.

### 2. You get more alcohol per glass than you think

As covered above, each cocktail is around 1.4 standard drinks. Hangover severity tracks closely with how much alcohol you drink and how high your blood alcohol gets. A sweet, cold, easy-to-drink cocktail that hides a lot of alcohol is close to an ideal recipe for overshooting.

### 3. Late caffeine wrecks your sleep

Caffeine has a half-life of around five hours in a typical healthy adult, though it ranges widely from person to person. That means if you have your last espresso martini at midnight, a good chunk of that caffeine is still active at 4 or 5 a.m.

Alcohol already disrupts sleep. It can make you fall asleep faster, but as your body processes it in the second half of the night, sleep becomes lighter and more broken, and you lose some deep sleep and REM sleep. (Our guide to [alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025) explains what happens hour by hour.) Add caffeine on top, and you get both problems at once: harder to fall asleep, and worse quality once you do.

Poor sleep makes almost every hangover symptom worse. Fatigue, brain fog, irritability, headache, and low mood are all amplified when you've slept badly. A lot of what people describe as a uniquely bad "espresso martini hangover" is really a normal hangover plus a short, broken night.

### 4. The jittery, anxious feeling

Some people wake up after espresso martinis feeling wired but exhausted, with a fast heartbeat and a sense of unease. A few things can contribute:

- **Leftover caffeine** if you drank late or are sensitive to it.
- **The alcohol rebound.** As alcohol wears off, the brain swings from being sedated to being overstimulated for a while. This is a big part of the shaky, anxious feeling sometimes called "hangxiety."
- **Dehydration and poor sleep**, which both raise heart rate a little.

For most social drinkers this fades within the day. If it feels intense, see our guides on [why your heart races after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) and on [alcohol and anxiety](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-anxiety-breaking-the-cycle-naturally-2025).

### 5. Sugar: a smaller factor than people think

Espresso martinis are sweet, and the coffee liqueur contributes a fair amount of sugar. It's common to hear that "sugar makes hangovers worse," but there is no good evidence that sugar in a cocktail meaningfully worsens a hangover on its own. The main effect of sugar is indirect: sweet drinks taste less like alcohol, so they're easier to drink quickly.

Very sugary drinks on an empty stomach can also leave some people with a mild energy crash and a queasy stomach. But if you drank the same amount of alcohol in an unsweetened drink, you'd still be hungover.

### 6. Congeners from the liqueur

Congeners are by-products of fermentation and aging that give some drinks their color and flavor. Research comparing bourbon to vodka, led by Damaris Rohsenow and published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2010, found that bourbon, which is high in congeners, produced somewhat worse hangovers than vodka at the same blood alcohol level, though the difference was modest.

Vodka is one of the lowest-congener spirits, which works in the espresso martini's favor. Coffee liqueurs are often rum-based and add some extra compounds, but the amount is small compared to a glass of whiskey or red wine. Congeners are probably a minor part of the picture here. Our [congeners guide](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) and [vodka hangover guide](/never-hungover/vodka-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) cover this in more detail.

## Does Caffeine Make a Hangover Worse?

It depends on when you have it.

**Caffeine the night before** probably does make the next morning worse, mostly through the routes above: it encourages more drinking and it cuts into sleep. Caffeine is also a mild diuretic, though in regular coffee drinkers that effect is small, and it's not a major cause of hangover dehydration compared to the alcohol itself.

**Caffeine the morning after** is a different story. If you normally drink coffee, skipping it on a hangover morning can add a caffeine-withdrawal headache on top of the hangover headache. A normal cup of coffee can take the edge off fatigue and help with that withdrawal piece. It won't fix the hangover, and too much can make an upset stomach or jitters worse, so stick to your usual amount and have water alongside it.

## Does Caffeine Sober You Up?

No. This is one of the most persistent myths about drinking, and espresso martinis feed right into it.

Your liver breaks down alcohol at a fairly steady rate, roughly one standard drink per hour for many people, though it varies. Nothing in an espresso changes that rate. Caffeine can make you feel more alert and less sleepy, but your judgment, reaction time, and coordination are still affected by whatever alcohol is in your blood.

That matters most for driving. Feeling "fine" after a couple of espresso martinis is exactly the situation where people overestimate how safe they are to drive. If you've been drinking, the coffee in your glass changes nothing about whether you should get behind the wheel.

## Is Mixing Caffeine and Alcohol Dangerous?

For most healthy adults, an occasional espresso martini or two is not dangerous in itself. The caffeine dose is similar to a cup of coffee.

The concern is about patterns, not one drink. In 2010, the US Food and Drug Administration sent warning letters to makers of premixed caffeinated alcoholic beverages (the original Four Loko era), saying the added caffeine was an unsafe additive in those products. Those drinks combined high alcohol content with high caffeine in one can, and they were linked to heavy, fast drinking. An espresso martini made at a bar is not the same product, but the reasoning behind the warning applies: caffeine makes it easier to drink more than you meant to.

Be more careful if you:

- Have a heart rhythm problem, high blood pressure, or have been told to limit caffeine
- Are prone to anxiety or panic attacks
- Take stimulant medications, such as some ADHD medicines
- Are pregnant or trying to become pregnant
- Are sensitive to caffeine in general and get jittery from a single coffee

If any of those apply, talk to your doctor about whether caffeinated cocktails fit your situation.

## How to Enjoy Espresso Martinis Without the Hangover

You don't need to give them up. A few adjustments make a big difference.

### Before you go out

- **Eat a proper meal.** Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol gets into your blood. A meal with some protein, fat, and fiber works better than a snack. Our [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) guide explains why.
- **Decide your number in advance.** Count each espresso martini as one and a half drinks. If your usual comfortable limit is three drinks, that's two espresso martinis.

### While you're drinking

- **Make it your last drink of the night only if the night is ending early.** Otherwise, have your espresso martini earlier and switch to something without caffeine. A good rule is no caffeine within about six hours of when you want to sleep, though sensitive people may need longer.
- **Alternate with water.** A glass of water between cocktails slows your pace and helps a little with hydration.
- **Ask for less sugar or a smaller pour.** Many bars will make a "skinny" version with less syrup, or a smaller serving. Less liqueur also means a little less alcohol.
- **Don't let the buzz from the caffeine decide whether you have another.** If you notice you feel surprisingly alert after a few, that's the caffeine talking, not your blood alcohol.
- **Try a decaf or zero-proof version.** Some bars will make an espresso martini with decaf espresso, which keeps the flavor and removes most of the caffeine. A non-alcoholic version made with espresso, a coffee syrup, and a little cream or tonic is also increasingly common.

### Before bed

- **Drink a glass or two of water**, not a liter. You want to rehydrate without being up all night.
- **Skip the "just in case" painkillers.** Taking acetaminophen while alcohol is still in your system isn't a good idea, and there's no evidence it prevents a hangover. See our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) for why.
- **Give yourself time to sleep.** If you can, plan for a later wake-up. Extra hours of sleep do more for a caffeine-and-alcohol hangover than almost anything else.

## How to Recover the Morning After

There's no instant cure, but you can make the day much easier.

1. **Rehydrate steadily.** Sip water throughout the morning. If you've been sick or sweaty, an electrolyte drink or oral rehydration solution can help you hold onto fluid better than plain water.
2. **Eat something gentle.** Toast, crackers, bananas, eggs, or a simple bowl of oats are easy on the stomach and help steady your blood sugar. [Eggs](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) are a popular choice for good reason.
3. **Have your normal amount of coffee, not double.** This heads off caffeine withdrawal without adding jitters. If your stomach is upset, try it after you've eaten something.
4. **Use a pain reliever carefully, if you need one.** Ibuprofen with food is often better for a hangover headache than acetaminophen, but it can irritate the stomach. Follow the label. Our [hangover headache guide](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025) covers the options.
5. **Nap if you can.** Because poor sleep is a big part of this particular hangover, a 20 to 30 minute nap in the early afternoon can help noticeably.
6. **Get some fresh air and light movement.** A short walk won't speed up alcohol clearance, but many people feel less foggy afterward.

Most hangovers peak in the morning and fade by the evening. If you're still feeling terrible the next day, or symptoms are getting worse instead of better, that's a reason to check in with a doctor.

## Espresso Martini vs Other Cocktails

Is an espresso martini hangover really worse than other cocktails? Gram for gram of alcohol, probably not by much. What makes it different is the combination of effects:

| Factor | Espresso martini | Vodka soda | Margarita | Red wine |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Alcohol per serving | High (about 1.4 standard drinks) | About 1 | Often 1.5 to 2 | About 1 per 5 oz |
| Caffeine | Yes, about a cup of coffee | None | None | None |
| Sugar | High | None | Moderate to high | Low |
| Congeners | Low (vodka) plus some from liqueur | Low | Low to moderate (tequila) | Higher |
| Main hangover driver | Extra drinking and poor sleep | Total alcohol | Total alcohol, sugar makes it easy to drink | Congeners, total alcohol |

The table is a general guide, not a precise ranking. Recipes and pours vary a lot. The takeaway is that the espresso martini's hangover reputation mostly comes from how it changes *your behavior and your sleep*, not from a special toxin in the drink.

## Do Hangover Supplements Help?

Some people take supplements before or after drinking to try to soften the next day. The honest view:

- **Electrolyte mixes** are useful if you're dehydrated, especially after vomiting or sweating. They don't address the alcohol itself.
- **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and on how alcohol acts in the brain. Most of the research is in animals and lab settings, with limited human data. Some people find it helpful, but there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers reliably in humans, and it does nothing about caffeine keeping you awake. If you want to try it, [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a good-value, single-ingredient option, and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) is a popular formula that adds electrolytes and other ingredients. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people typically use it, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare brands.
- **Any supplement is a small add-on at best.** The things that make the biggest difference are still drinking less, eating, pacing yourself, and getting enough sleep. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) puts the evidence in order.

No supplement makes it safe to drink more, and none of them change your blood alcohol level for driving purposes.

## The Bottom Line

- An espresso martini is roughly **1.4 standard drinks**, not one. Count it that way.
- The caffeine **doesn't sober you up**. It makes you feel less drunk, which makes it easy to drink more.
- Late-night caffeine plus alcohol means **worse sleep**, and poor sleep makes every hangover symptom worse.
- Sugar and congeners play **smaller roles** than people think.
- Have your espresso martini earlier in the night, alternate with water, eat first, and keep your usual morning coffee to avoid a withdrawal headache.
- If someone is confused, can't stay awake, or is breathing slowly after drinking, call 911. Caffeine doesn't protect against alcohol poisoning.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why do espresso martinis give me such a bad hangover?**

Mostly because each one holds about 1.4 standard drinks, the caffeine makes you feel less drunk so you tend to drink more, and late-night caffeine plus alcohol leads to short, broken sleep. Poor sleep makes headache, fatigue, and brain fog worse. Sugar and congeners play smaller roles.

**Does the caffeine in an espresso martini sober you up?**

No. Caffeine doesn't change how fast your liver clears alcohol or lower your blood alcohol level. It only makes you feel more alert. Your judgment, reaction time, and coordination are still impaired, so an espresso martini never makes it safe to drive.

**How many standard drinks are in an espresso martini?**

A classic recipe with about 50 ml of vodka and 25 ml of coffee liqueur contains roughly 19 to 20 grams of alcohol, or about 1.4 US standard drinks. Larger pours or stronger liqueurs can push it toward two.

**How much caffeine is in an espresso martini?**

Usually about 60 to 75 mg from the espresso shot, plus a small amount from the coffee liqueur. That's roughly the same as a small cup of coffee. Two or three in an evening adds up to a full morning's worth of caffeine taken late at night.

**Is it dangerous to mix caffeine and alcohol?**

For most healthy adults, an occasional espresso martini isn't dangerous on its own. The main risk is that caffeine masks how drunk you feel, which can lead to heavier drinking. People with heart rhythm problems, high blood pressure, anxiety disorders, or who take stimulant medication should ask their doctor first.

**Should I drink coffee the morning after espresso martinis?**

If you normally drink coffee, yes, have your usual amount. Skipping it can add a caffeine-withdrawal headache on top of the hangover. Don't double up, have it with water, and try it after eating if your stomach is upset.

**Does sugar make an espresso martini hangover worse?**

There is no good evidence that the sugar itself meaningfully worsens a hangover. Its main effect is that sweet drinks taste less boozy and go down faster, so you may drink more alcohol than you realize.

**How can I avoid a hangover from espresso martinis?**

Eat a real meal first, count each one as one and a half drinks, alternate with water, and have your last caffeinated cocktail about six hours before bed. Asking for less syrup, a smaller pour, or decaf espresso also helps. Drinking less is still the most reliable fix.
